procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention under s. 3(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not Applicable. The case originated as a writ petition directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a petition under Art. 32 of the Constitution challenging his detention on the ground that the State Government did not consider his representation of June 23, 1969 with reasonable and proper expedition. The Supreme Court allowed the petition and set the petitioner at liberty.

directions: The petitioner is set at liberty.
The petitioner is ordered to be released forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether the State Government's delay in considering the petitioner's representation violated his constitutional rights, thereby invalidating the detention order.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, on June 7, 1969.
He submitted a representation to the State Government on June 23, 1969.
The State Government placed the case, including the representation, before an Advisory Board on July 1, 1969.
The Advisory Board gave its opinion on August 13, 1969, finding sufficient cause for detention.
The State Government allegedly rejected the petitioner's representation on August 19, 1969, and the Governor confirmed the detention on August 26, 1969.
The State Government argued that the delay was due to an inquiry it conducted through the Superintendent of Railway Police, whose report was delayed.
law: The Court established that the appropriate government has a constitutional obligation, implicit in Article 22 of the Constitution, to consider a detenu's representation as expeditiously as possible.
This duty is imperative because the personal liberty of a citizen is at stake.
The government's consideration of the representation must be independent of the opinion of the Advisory Board.
application: The Court found that there was an "inordinate delay" between the petitioner's representation on June 23 and its consideration by the government on August 19.
The State Government failed to provide any explanation for this long delay. It did not specify when the police inquiry was ordered, how long it took, or why it was necessary.
The officer who allegedly conducted the inquiry did not file an affidavit to support the State's claim.

The Court also found it problematic that the government put off considering the representation until after it had received the opinion of the Advisory Board. This raised doubts as to whether the government had exercised its own "independent judgment" as required by the Constitution.
The Court concluded that the State's inactivity and lack of independent judgment constituted a failure to discharge its constitutional obligation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's argument, ruling that the State Government's unexplained and inordinate delay in considering the representation, combined with its failure to consider it independently of the Advisory Board's report, violated the petitioner's constitutional rights. This failure invalidated the detention order, and the Court ordered the petitioner to be set at liberty.

issue.issue_text: Whether the government is constitutionally obligated to dispose of a representation from a detenu with utmost expedition.

facts: A detenu filed a representation on June 23, 1969, challenging their detention.
The State Government rejected this representation on August 19, 1969, after the Advisory Board had made its report.
The government contended that it had fulfilled its duty by considering the representation after making its own enquiries and receiving the Advisory Board's report.
The detenu argued that the government did not consider the representation with reasonable and proper expedition, thus violating their rights.
law: Article 22 of the Constitution guarantees a detenu the fundamental right to make a representation and to have it considered by the appropriate authority.
This constitutional right implies that the government is obligated to consider the representation as early and as expeditiously as possible.
The consideration of the representation by the government is an independent duty, separate from any review by an Advisory Board.
Any delay in considering the representation is not only an irresponsible act but is unconstitutional because the personal liberty of a person is at stake.
application: The Court established that the government's duty is not merely to forward the representation to an Advisory Board but to conduct its own independent and prompt review.
The Court reasoned that the fundamental right to have a representation considered would be "rendered meaningless" if the government could deal with it at its own convenience rather than with urgency.
Citing precedent, the Court emphasized that the government has a legal obligation to consider the representation "as soon as it is received by it."

The Court found that a delay of nearly two months, and disposing of the representation only after the Advisory Board's report, raised doubts about whether the government had performed its independent constitutional duty in an expeditious manner.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that the government is under a constitutional obligation, stemming from the fundamental right to personal liberty in Article 22, to consider and dispose of a detenu's representation with the utmost expedition. Any inordinate delay violates this constitutional guarantee.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the State Government's delay in considering the petitioner's representation violated his constitutional rights, thereby invalidating the detention order.
appellant_arguments: The government did not consider the petitioner's representation, made on June 23, 1969, with reasonable and proper expedition.
The government improperly delayed the consideration of the representation until after it had received the opinion of the Advisory Board.
respondent_arguments: The government discharged its duty by referring the matter and the representation to the Advisory Board, and then rejecting the representation on August 19, 1969.
The government made inquiries after receiving the representation, which accounts for the time taken to consider it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the government is constitutionally obligated to dispose of a representation from a detenu with utmost expedition.
appellant_arguments: The government's failure to consider the representation with reasonable and proper expedition is a violation of the detenu's constitutional rights, implying an obligation to act swiftly.
respondent_arguments: The government fulfilled its duty by considering the representation after the Advisory Board's report, implying that the procedural steps are what matter, not the speed of consideration.

cases.case_name: Sk. Abdul Karim & Ors. v. The State of West Bengal
cases.principle: The appropriate Government cannot be said to discharge its obligation merely by forwarding the representation of the detenu to the Advisory Board; Article 22 of the Constitution guarantees the right of a detenu to have a proper consideration of the representation by the appropriate authority itself.

cases.case_name: Pankaj Kumar Chakrabarty & Ors. v. The State of West Bengal
cases.principle: The obligation of the appropriate authority to consider the detenu's representation under section 7 of the Act is entirely independent of any action by the Advisory Board. The representation is addressed to the Government so that it can exercise its own opinion and judgment in an independent and honest manner.

cases.case_name: Khairul Haque v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: It was applied to support the conclusion that the appropriate authority failed to discharge its constitutional obligation by inactivity and lack of independent judgment in considering the detenu's representation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The appropriate government has a constitutional obligation to consider a detenu's representation as expeditiously as possible. Any inordinate delay in this consideration, including postponing it until after receiving the opinion of the Advisory Board, is an unconstitutional violation of the detenu's fundamental right.
obiter: The reason for immediate consideration of the representation is that the personal liberty of a person is at stake.
Even if the Advisory Board expresses an opinion against the release of a detenu, the government may still exercise its power to release the detenu.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The State of West Bengal was guilty of an infraction of constitutional provisions. The court's inescapable conclusion was that the appropriate authority failed to discharge its constitutional obligation through both inactivity and a lack of independent judgment. This failure was demonstrated not only by the inordinate and unexplained delay in reviewing the petitioner's representation but also by putting off its consideration until after receiving the opinion of the Advisory Board.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the appropriate Government has disposed of the case as expeditiously as possible, as it is bound to consider the representation of the detenu as early as possible.

Whether the appropriate Government exercised its own opinion and judgment on the representation before sending the case to the Advisory Board, as it must consider the representation uninfluenced by any opinion or consideration of the Board.
policy_considerations: The personal liberty of a person is at stake, and any delay is not only an irresponsible act but also unconstitutional because the Constitution enshrines the fundamental right of a detenu to have his representation considered.
When the liberty of a person is in peril, it is imperative that immediate action should be taken by the relevant authorities.
A citizen's right raises a correlative duty of the State.

The constitutional right to have a representation considered by the appropriate Government would be rendered meaningless if the Government does not deal with the matter expeditiously but at its own sweet will and convenience.
